opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we've honestly gone back and forth on a lot internally, and I'll admit we haven't always gotten it right. Our naming has been confusing at times, and people have rightly given us a hard time about it.

The old mental model was that you train a big model, release it, give it a number, and then a year or two later you train a bigger one and bump the number. That fit a world where progress came in big discrete jumps. But that's increasingly not how it works. Now we're continually post-training, improving reasoning, updating the model's behavior, adding new capabilities, sometimes on a timescale of weeks. The thing you're talking to in month six might be meaningfully better than what launched in month one, even if it has the same name.

So I think naming has to do two jobs that are somewhat in tension. One is giving people a stable sense of "this is the generation of system I'm using." That's useful, especially for developers who need to build on something predictable. The other is being honest that the system is a living thing that keeps getting better. I don't think you want a new big number every time you ship an improvement. That would be exhausting and would make the numbers meaningless.

Where I've landed, at least for now, is that big version numbers should mark real step changes, the kind where people feel a qualitative difference in what's possible. Within a generation you do more continuous, quieter updates, with clear communication about what changed. For developers you keep pinned, dated snapshots so nobody's product breaks overnight.

Longer term, I hope most people won't think about model names at all. You'll just use ChatGPT and it'll get smarter, and the right model will get picked for what you're doing. Model names are kind of an artifact of this moment, and ideally they fade into the background.

r001.rationale: It contrasts discrete releases of newly trained models with continual post-training, noting that a model can improve substantially while keeping the same name.

r002.rationale: It describes the tension between keeping a stable generation name and assigning new numbers to ongoing improvements, and says not to issue a new big number for every update.

r003.rationale: It mentions pinned, dated snapshots so developers’ products remain predictable, but does not clearly identify users’ desire to keep using a preferred snapshot after updates.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that our naming has been a mess, and we know it. Part of why it got messy is that the way models improve changed underneath us, and the names didn't keep up.

The old mental model was that a model was a discrete artifact. You trained GPT-3, you shipped it, it sat there, and then a couple of years later you trained GPT-4 and that was a new thing. A version number made sense for that world. It was like a software release.

That's not really how it works anymore. The systems improve continuously now. We're doing post-training updates, we're adding tools, we're changing how much the model thinks before it answers, and a model you use in March can be meaningfully better than the "same" model in January. So a static number on the box is a little misleading. It tells you about a training run, not about what you're actually getting today.

So the way I think about it is that the name should reflect capability and intent, not internal history. People shouldn't have to know what "o" versus "4.5" versus "mini" means. They should be able to say, roughly, "I want the fastest one" or "I want the smartest one and I'll wait," and the naming should make that obvious. Ideally you don't pick a model at all, and the system figures out how much to think based on the question.

I also think we should get comfortable with the idea that a major version is more like an era than a product. GPT-5 shouldn't mean one frozen checkpoint. It should mean a family that keeps getting better, where the number signals a step change in what's possible and the improvements inside that era just show up without you needing to track them.

The tension is that people, and especially developers, legitimately want stability. If you're building on us you need to know something won't shift under you. So I think you end up with two layers. A simple, human-facing name that tracks the era and the tier, and then underneath it a boring, dated, pinned version for people who need reproducibility. We've been bad at keeping those two layers clean, and that's on us.

If I had to boil it down, naming should get simpler as the technology gets more complex. The fact that we went the other direction for a while is a sign we were naming things for ourselves instead of for the people using them.

r001.rationale: It contrasts discrete trained releases with continuous improvement through post-training updates, making version boundaries less clear.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a continuing major-version family with dated, pinned versions beneath it, addressing whether updates keep a shared name or get distinct version identifiers.

r003.rationale: It mentions developers’ need for stability and reproducibility, but does not clearly state that users want to keep using a preferred snapshot after later updates.

astra-6.text:
I think the naming should make it easier to understand what you’re getting. Historically, a new model name has signaled this big, discrete jump. But these systems increasingly improve through lots of smaller updates, and a name alone doesn’t communicate all of that very well.

There are really two needs: most people want to open the product and have it work as well as possible, without thinking about which model to pick. Developers and researchers need to know exactly which version they’re using, what changed, and whether they can reproduce a result. I’d like us to make the everyday experience simpler while keeping that precision available.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts discrete historical jumps with smaller ongoing updates, but does not explain that continual post-training blurs boundaries compared with newly trained models.

r002.rationale: It calls for knowing the exact version and what changed, but does not raise whether updates should keep the same name or receive distinct version numbers.

r003.rationale: It mentions reproducibility needs, but does not identify users’ desire to keep using a preferred model snapshot after later updates.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the naming should make it easier to understand what you’re getting. The old model was: we train a model, give it a number, release it, and then eventually release the next one. But if these systems improve more continuously, that starts to feel like an awkward fit.

You still want meaningful milestones, so people can understand when there’s been a big jump. But you also want some way to communicate what’s changed along the way. And ideally, you shouldn’t need to study our naming system to figure out which model to use. We should make that much simpler.
